rationale: A wins because it keeps the reporting burden inside the facts and turns missing data into a legitimate story: "REI won't say how much of its business is used gear" is sharp, if slightly overstated. B has usable bones, but "As outdoor gear floods secondhand apps" drags in a whole marketplace premise the update never gave it. That is how a decent angle set walks itself into a correction before the first email goes out.
gaps_in_A: "REI won't say how much of its business is used gear" overstates "not disclosed" into an active refusal unless REI has actually declined to answer.

"every store needs intake space, grading standards, technicians, and inventory handling" assumes the operating model before proving whether stores do full service, intake-only, hubs, or third parties.
"a public retailer answering to shareholders has a hard time cheering on resale" is a smart hypothesis, but it is not in the update and needs outside proof before it becomes the spine of a pitch.
gaps_in_B: "As outdoor gear floods secondhand apps" is invented color. The update gives no secondhand-app trend, volume data, or competitive platform evidence.
"public retailers can't easily replicate" is too big for the supplied facts. It turns an ownership-structure hypothesis into a headline claim.
"putting a number on what co-op membership is worth" collapses without the actual dividend amount, and trade-in credit is not automatically membership value.
"requires trained repair technicians — a skilled, non-automatable role" assumes store-level staffing and job design that the update does not establish.
